https://vietnam.vnanet.vn/english/tin-va.text: In the News Key Party leader hosts Hungarian Workers’ Party chief 06/10/2026 Politburo Member and Standing Member of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) Central Committee’s Secretariat Tran Cam Tu hosted a reception in Hanoi on October 5 for a delegation of the Hungarian Workers’ Party. Politburo Member and Standing Member of the Communist Party of Vietnam Central Committee’s Secretariat Tran Cam Tu receives in Hanoi on October 5 a delegation of the Hungarian Workers’ Party led by its President Gyula Thürmer. Photo: VNA Politburo Member and Standing Member of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) Central Committee’s Secretariat Tran Cam Tu hosted a reception in Hanoi on October 5 for a delegation of the Hungarian Workers’ Party led by its President Gyula Thürmer, who is on a working trip to Vietnam from October 4-10. The host conveyed best wishes from General Secretary of the CPV Central Committee and President To Lam to the delegation. He praised years of solidarity, friendship and cooperation between the two Parties and countries, stressing that the Vietnamese Party, State and people always value and are grateful for the selfless, wholehearted and faithful support of Hungarian communists and people to Vietnam in the past struggle for national liberation and reunification, and in the current national construction and defence. He welcomed the Hungarian Workers’ Party’s achievements, especially its steadfast commitment to ideals and Marxism-Leninism. He believed that the Party would keep consolidating its organisation, renewing its operating methods, raising its prestige and standing, and actively contributing to Hungary’s development and higher living standards. The key Party leader affirmed Vietnam’s determination to meet two 100-year goals of becoming a developing, upper-middle-income country with modern industry by 2030, and a developed, high-income country by 2045. Reaching those targets requires Party building and rectification as a key task, tied to strengthening the Party's leadership, governing capacity and combat strength, and overhauling its leadership methods. All policies are people-centred, linking economic growth with cultural development, upholding discipline and ensuring citizens' security, safety and well-being, he said. Vietnam will stay on the path to socialism and pursue the foreign policy of independence, self-reliance, peace, friendship, cooperation, development, diversification and multilateralisation of external ties, and active, proactive global integration, he said. He added that the CPV always values its solidarity and friendship with the Hungarian Workers' Party and communist and workers' parties worldwide, which helps build political trust and supports Vietnam's relations with other countries. Thürmer, in reply, said he is pleased to return to Vietnam and again congratulated General Secretary and President Lam on his election as Party chief for the 14th term. He praised Vietnam's achievements after 40 years of Doi moi (Renewal), calling them clear proof of the CPV's sound leadership and a source of encouragement and valuable experience for his Party and the international communist and workers' movement. Sharing orientations on Party building and consolidation and praising Vietnam’s foreign policy, Thürmer affirmed that steadfast adherence to Marxism-Leninism is the right choice for communist parties, and believed that Vietnam would successfully achieve its development goals through 2030 and its vision to 2045. Citing Vietnam's growing role and standing in the region and the world, he said the Hungarian Workers' Party and other Hungarian political parties support the government's efforts to deepen the traditional friendship and multifaceted cooperation with Vietnam in an increasingly close and substantive way. The two sides agreed on five cooperation priorities and more delegation exchanges at all levels and between the parties' advisory bodies. They shared experience in Party building and pledged to use the Party channel to boost cooperation in areas where both have strengths, while giving attention to traditional fields such as education-training, culture and people-to-people exchanges, to strengthen the social foundation for bilateral ties for the benefit of the two countries' people. The discussions helped tighten solidarity between the two Parties, clarify the direction of long-term cooperation and elevate the role of Party diplomacy in deepening the Vietnam-Hungary Comprehensive Partnership./. Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA View image in fullscreen Students at a protest in Prague on Tuesday in support of the public broadcasters. Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA Czechia Protest in Prague over media freedom expected to be one of biggest in Czechia’s history Hundreds of thousands expected to rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget Rory Carroll Sun 15 Nov 2026 06.17 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.19 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of thousands of Czechs are expected to rally in Prague on Sunday to protest against what they say is a government attempt to stifle media freedom. The gathering to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters could be one of the biggest in the country’s history, organisers say. It will mark the latest challenge to the prime minister, Andrej Babiš, and his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, and follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio. Public media freedom has been eroded across central Europe. Now Czechs are rallying to protect theirs Read more Protesters say the plan to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters from the state budget would give ministers more leverage over newsrooms and follow the example of Slovakia , Hungary, Poland and Serbia, where current and previous rightwing populist governments eroded media independence. The Million Moments for Democracy group that is organising the demonstration said the authorities would see the level of opposition. “Babiš and his government obviously think they will get away with anything … that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property,” it said. The group expects 400,000 to 600,000 people at Letná Plain, which overlooks Prague’s historic centre. Some protesters would be channelling wider opposition to the government, said Daniel Stach, a TV presenter and one of the most recognised faces of the campaign. The proposed changes, which would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%, have drawn fire from international media organisations. The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have also criticised the government’s media plan, likening it to controversial moves by Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico , and Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán . Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were riling up the public with unfounded claims about threats to media freedom. Last week, he published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month. “Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.” Explore more on these topics Czechia Press freedom Europe Protest Newspapers & magazines news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Trumpist’ Czech PM-elect refuses to sell business empire amid conflict-of-interest row Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr When Czech populists win, that’s nothing peculiarly ‘east European’. https://www.politico.eu/article/russian-.text: DNIPRO, Ukraine — Heavy Russian losses are one of the reasons for Moscow’s slowing advance in Ukraine this year, the commander of the country’s Air Assault Forces said. “Even though the Russian offensive continues, the enemy is not demonstrating rapid operational successes that would allow it to advance quickly. They are slowing down,” Maj. Gen. Oleh Apostol told a group of journalists in a secure location on Tuesday. "If they capture a single tree line in a month, that hardly constitutes an operational success upon which further gains can be built," Apostol said. Advertisement Advertisement Russian casualties are rising, according to the commander and to NATO officials. “In the past few months, Russia has been losing more than 40,000 troops — killed or seriously wounded — every month. The United States in 14 years, in Vietnam, lost 56,000. Here in one month, Russia, dead or seriously wounded, 40,000. And in October, early reporting indicates this number may have climbed to over 50,000,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said this week. Neither Ukraine nor Russia publishes their exact military losses. The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies this summer estimated that Russian forces had suffered about 1.4 million casualties, including 400,000 to 450,000 fatalities, from the start of the full-scale invasion through June 2026. It estimated Ukrainian casualties at 525,000 to 625,000, including 125,000 to 150,000 fatalities, over the same period. Despite rising casualties, the Russian military continues to press forward but is making few lasting gains, Apostol said. He estimated that Ukrainian forces had retaken more than 800 square kilometers from Russian forces this year as the result of two local counteroffensive operations. Ukraine’s offensives have both a military and a political meaning as they show Kyiv is successfully resisting Russian pressure, Apostol said. Advertisement Advertisement In his view, successes on the battlefield provide additional arguments for continuing military aid from Kyiv's allies, while a lack of positive momentum could increase external pressure to negotiate. “Ukrainian counter-offensive actions refute Russian claims regarding the impossibility of further resistance and strengthen Ukraine’s arguments in its engagement with international partners,” the general said. Apostol said that many of Moscow's claimed successes are propaganda efforts that do not mark real territorial gains and that lower-level commanders may mislead their superiors about the actual situation on the battlefield. When it’s impossible to demonstrate real success, Russian forces use individual soldiers with flags to film proof of control over entire areas, Apostol said, adding that such soldiers are usually quickly killed by Ukrainian forces. “A Russian flag at a given position does not necessarily mean that the location has actually been captured and is being held,” he said. Claims and counter-claims During the latest round of U.S.-led peace talks this week, Russia claimed it had occupied half of the territory in the Donbas that is currently under Ukrainian control, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . Advertisement Advertisement "So the Russians think and they share that they really occupied half of the territory of Donbas, which we control really," he said, adding that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was being misinformed and that Kremlin negotiators were trying to use exaggerated territorial claims to influence the U.S. "I think that Putin lives a little bit in different information," Zelenskyy said. "It's a different reality. And of course, he is sharing with America." Russia is claiming that it has taken 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while the Institute for the Study of War think tank estimates that the real total is a Russian net gain of only 73 square kilometers. Putin is "trying once again to breathe life into the myth of inevitable Russian military victory in order to persuade the United States and other supporters of Ukraine to compel Kyiv to surrender," ISW wrote. Apostol underlined that Ukraine is being very careful in its operations to try and minimize troop losses because of its lack of manpower. “You must attack where success is possible,” Apostol said, adding that Ukraine favors localized attacks instead of a massive counteroffensive. In many cases, the goal is to stabilize the frontline and not to take more territory. “Launching an offensive against a well-prepared enemy force that holds a numerical advantage may fail to yield the desired outcome,” he said. Ukraine has a much smaller population than Russia and has had difficulties in recruiting new forces and preventing soldiers from deserting. "If a person is treated like a dog, they might go AWOL," Apostol said. Advertisement Advertisement
